strengths: The paper addresses a significant open gap in online structured prediction: while prior surrogate regret guarantees break down under non-stationarity (yielding vacuous $\Omega(T)$ cumulative target loss), this work establishes a non-trivial small-surrogate-loss + path-length bound of $F_T + O(1 + P_T)$ holding for any comparator sequence.

The technical development is clean and elegant: combining the dynamic regret analysis of OGD with surrogate-gap techniques provides an intuitive mechanism for deriving cumulative target-loss bounds, and naturally suggests an adaptive Polyak-style learning rate.

The extension in Section 4 to convolutional Fenchel–Young losses significantly broadens the applicable scope to settings where the prediction space and label space differ (such as ranking with NDCG loss), supported by new technical lemmas (Lemmas 4.3 and 4.4) linking target loss, surrogate loss, and gradient norms.

The theoretical characterization is comprehensive, including a matching $\Omega(F_T + P_T)$ lower bound demonstrating the worst-case optimality of the joint linear dependence on surrogate loss and path length.
The manuscript is clearly written, logically organized, and transparent about its assumptions, proofs, and limitations.
weaknesses: The core analysis in Section 3 is relatively straightforward once Proposition 2.4 and the surrogate gap condition are combined, as the step-size condition directly cancels the surrogate loss terms.

The empirical evaluation is somewhat limited: experiments are conducted only on simple classification settings (2D synthetic data and 3-class MNIST with label flips), leaving the performance on richer structured prediction problems (such as ranking with NDCG loss, which was theoretically developed in Section 4) unverified experimentally.
The setting is currently restricted to full-information feedback, whereas several recent works on stationary online structured prediction have moved toward bandit or semi-bandit feedback.

strengths: The paper provides a significant and clean theoretical contribution by establishing a cumulative target-loss bound of the form $F_T + O(1 + P_T)$ for online structured prediction in non-stationary environments, effectively removing the explicit horizon $T$ dependence that hindered previous surrogate regret bounds.

The theoretical framework is broad and goes beyond prior online surrogate regret work (which required $\hat{\mathcal{Y}} = \mathcal{Y}$) by leveraging convolutional Fenchel–Young losses, supported by novel technical lemmas (Lemma 4.3 and Lemma 4.4) connecting the target loss, surrogate loss, and gradient norms.

The paper proves a matching $\Omega(F_T + P_T)$ lower bound via Yao's minimax principle, establishing the minimax optimality of the joint linear dependence on path length and cumulative surrogate loss.

The proposed Polyak-style learning rate is mathematically well-motivated by the dynamic regret analysis, avoids overly conservative constant step sizes, and shows clear empirical gains over standard baselines (constant and AdaGrad) as non-stationarity increases.

The paper is very well written, mathematically rigorous, and provides insightful corrections and discussions of prior literature (such as the convexity and self-bounding issues regarding the multiclass hinge loss in Appendix C).
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is restricted to relatively small-scale multiclass classification problems (synthetic data and 3-class MNIST with segment flips) rather than complex structured prediction tasks (such as ranking with NDCG loss) where the convolutional Fenchel–Young framework is especially relevant.
The setting is strictly restricted to full-information feedback; extending such dynamic guarantees to bandit or semi-bandit feedback remains an open challenge.

The computational overhead per round for general structured prediction can be non-negligible, as the randomized decoding and the Polyak-style step size calculation require iterative Frank–Wolfe optimization with linear minimization oracles.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated conceptual contribution: Bridges dynamic regret in online convex optimization with the exploit-the-surrogate-gap literature in online structured prediction, addressing a key limitation where static surrogate regret bounds degenerate to Omega(T) under non-stationarity.

Strong and clean theoretical guarantees: Establishes a target loss bound of the form F_T + O(1 + P_T) that holds for any time-varying comparator sequence without needing prior knowledge of T or the path length P_T, recovering classical finite bounds when P_T = 0.

Extension to general structured prediction tasks: Extends beyond standard settings where the prediction space matches the label space by leveraging convolutional Fenchel–Young losses (e.g., for NDCG ranking), supported by novel technical lemmas (Lemmas 4.3 and 4.4) on the surrogate-target gap and quadratic growth.
Tightness: Establishes a matching Omega(F_T + P_T) lower bound, showing that the joint linear dependence on surrogate loss and path length is optimal in the worst case.

Practical stepsize design: The surrogate-gap analysis naturally yields a Polyak-style adaptive learning rate that is computationally viable via Frank–Wolfe oracles and empirically outperforms static or standard AdaGrad stepsizes in non-stationary environments.
weaknesses: Relies on standard OGD mechanics: Once the surrogate-gap cancellation and learning-rate condition (Equation 4) are formulated, the core OGD dynamic regret reduction relies fairly directly on classical analyses (e.g., Zinkevich / Hall & Willett).

Restriction to full-information feedback: The theoretical guarantees rely heavily on full feedback of y_t to evaluate gradients and target losses; extending this to bandit or semi-bandit structured prediction remains an open and challenging question.

Scope of empirical evaluation: While Section 4 and Appendix B.3 provide detailed theoretical formulations for complex structured prediction (e.g., NDCG ranking via Birkhoff polytope projections), the numerical experiments are limited to 2-class synthetic and 3-class MNIST classification.

Assumption of bounded domain: The analysis requires a compact parameter domain W with diameter D and explicit projections onto W, which may introduce tuning overhead for D in unconstrained applications.

strengths: The paper addresses a significant limitation of existing surrogate regret bounds in online structured prediction, which degrade to trivial linear bounds in non-stationary environments, by establishing tight 'small-surrogate-loss + path-length' bounds of the form $F_T + C(1 + P_T)$.

The theoretical framework is clean and elegant: synthesizing Zinkevich's dynamic regret analysis for OGD with non-increasing step sizes and surrogate-gap cancellation properties yields transparent and powerful guarantees.

The extension to general structured prediction problems (where the label space and prediction space differ, such as NDCG ranking) via the convolutional Fenchel–Young loss is novel, supported by key technical lemmas (Lemmas 4.3 and 4.4) that bypass standard affine-decomposability and separation requirements.

The paper provides insightful side observations, notably pointing out and clarifying technical flaws in prior work regarding the discontinuity or non-self-bounding nature of previously used multiclass hinge loss variants (Appendix C).
The presentation and mathematical writing are exceptionally clear, rigorous, and well-organized throughout the manuscript.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is very preliminary: it is restricted to a 2D synthetic binary classification problem with label flips. Given that the paper focuses on structured prediction (and introduces machinery for convolutional Fenchel–Young losses for ranking/multilabel tasks), the lack of empirical evaluation on structured prediction benchmarks (e.g., ranking or sequence labeling) weakens the practical demonstration.

The step-size rule in (5) is constrained to be non-increasing over time ($\eta_t = \min(\dots, \eta_{t-1})$) to satisfy the dynamic OGD regret analysis. In non-stationary environments with recurrent shifts over very long horizons, being unable to increase the learning rate after a transient shock may hinder tracking performance, even though it remains bounded below by $\alpha/M$.

strengths: Addresses an important limitation in online structured prediction and online classification: while existing surrogate-regret bounds are finite in stationary environments, they become vacuous when non-stationarity causes any static comparator to incur linear surrogate loss. The paper establishes clean 'small-surrogate-loss + path-length' bounds of the form $F_T + C(1 + P_T)$.

The technical synthesis between dynamic regret analysis of OGD and the surrogate-gap property is elegant, conceptually transparent, and leads directly to an insightful Polyak-style adaptive learning rate.

The extension to convolutional Fenchel–Young losses in Section 4 is technically non-trivial and substantially widens the applicability of the framework to settings where label and prediction spaces differ (such as document ranking under NDCG loss), supported by novel target–surrogate relationship lemmas (Lemmas 4.3 and 4.4).
The theoretical analysis is complemented by a matching lower bound (Theorem 5.1), proving that the linear dependence on both $F_T$ and $P_T$ cannot be improved in the worst case.
The paper is very well-written, logically structured, and provides transparent proofs and discussions throughout the manuscript.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is limited to a simple synthetic 2D binary classification setup with segment-wise label flips. Evaluating on an actual structured prediction benchmark (e.g., the NDCG ranking problem highlighted in Section 4 and Appendix B.3) would have considerably strengthened the practical relevance of the findings.

The dynamic regret analysis relies on a known compact domain with bounded diameter $D$ (Assumption 2.2). While common in dynamic OCO, some stationary structured prediction methods can adapt to unknown domain sizes, leaving domain adaptation in the dynamic setting as an unaddressed challenge.

The guarantees are restricted strictly to full-information feedback, whereas bandit feedback is standard and practically relevant in many structured prediction applications (though the authors appropriately acknowledge this limitation).

strengths: Addresses an important and fundamental limitation in online structured prediction: while existing literature achieves impressive finite surrogate regret bounds, these guarantees degrade to Omega(T) in non-stationary environments. The paper successfully remedies this with dynamic guarantees.

The theoretical framework is elegant and mathematically sound. Synthesizing the dynamic regret analysis of OGD (generalized here to non-increasing learning rates in Proposition 2.4) with the surrogate gap technique yields a clean and interpretable cumulative target loss bound of FT + C(1 + PT).

Extends beyond standard structured prediction assumptions (where label and prediction spaces are identical) to convolutional Fenchel-Young losses. The newly developed target-surrogate relations (Lemmas 4.3 and 4.4) are technically novel and enable guarantees for problems like ranking under NDCG loss.
Proposes a well-motivated Polyak-style adaptive learning rate that systematically respects the theoretical conditions while exhibiting strong empirical adaptability in non-stationary regimes.

Provides a matching lower bound (Theorem 5.1) confirming that the linear dependencies on both the cumulative surrogate loss FT and path length PT are worst-case optimal, and provides valuable technical clarification on previous formulations of the multiclass hinge loss (Appendix C).
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is primarily restricted to synthetic 2D binary classification with artificial label flips (Appendix E). Demonstrating the Polyak-style learning rate on high-dimensional, real-world structured prediction tasks (e.g., document ranking or sequence labeling) would significantly strengthen the empirical claims.

The theoretical guarantees are confined to the full-information feedback setting. While extending dynamic surrogate regret bounds to bandit or partial-information structured prediction is technically challenging, it remains a notable practical limitation.

Implementation of the algorithmic framework and choice of theoretical learning rates require prior knowledge of problem-dependent parameters such as domain diameter D and strong convexity/smoothness constants M and lambda.
